bib.title: Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation

question: Can a policy represented by its own function approximator be updated by the gradient of expected reward, with that gradient estimated from experience using a learned approximate value function, and does this converge?
hypothesis: A learned approximate action-value or advantage function satisfying a compatibility condition gives an unbiased policy-gradient estimate, so policy iteration with function approximation converges to a local optimum.
contributions: Policy Gradient Theorem (Theorem 1): gradient of performance has no state-distribution derivative term
Theorem 2: gradient is exact when the approximate Q (f_w) is compatible with the policy parameterization and at a local optimum of its fit
Theorem 3: first proof that a form of policy iteration with general differentiable function approximation converges to a locally optimal policy

results.claim: Policy gradient theorem: the gradient of performance equals the sum over states and actions of d(s) dpi/dtheta Q, with no term for the derivative of the state distribution.
results.setup: Any MDP, average-reward or start-state formulation; pi differentiable in theta.
results.quote: the key point is that their are no terms of the form ∂dπ(s) ∂θ : the eﬀect of policy changes on the distribution of states does not appear.

results.claim: With f_w compatible with the policy (df/dw = dpi/dtheta / pi) and converged in least squares, substituting f_w for Q gives the exact gradient.
results.quote: which tells us that the error in fw(s, a) is orthogonal to the gradient of the policy parameterization.

results.claim: For a Gibbs (softmax) policy linear in features, the compatible f_w is linear in the same features, mean-centred per state, so it approximates the advantage function.
results.quote: In other words, fw must be linear in the same features as the policy, except normalized to be mean zero for each state.

results.claim: Adding any state-only function v(s) (a baseline) leaves the gradient theorems unchanged but can change estimator variance.
results.setup: Because sum_a dpi/dtheta = 0 for every state.
results.quote: The choice of v does not aﬀect any of our theorems, but can substantially aﬀect the variance of the gradient estimators.

results.claim: Policy iteration with compatible differentiable approximators converges to a point where the gradient is zero, under bounded second derivatives, bounded rewards and standard step sizes.
results.setup: Theorem 3: max|d2pi/dtheta_i dtheta_j| < B, step sizes alpha_k -> 0 and sum alpha_k = infinity; relies on Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis (1996) Prop 3.5 p96.

results.claim: REINFORCE gives an unbiased gradient estimate without a value function but learns much more slowly; a learned value function to cut variance appears essential for rapid learning (asserted, no experiment).
results.setup: Comparison with Williams 1988/1992 REINFORCE; no experiments in the paper.
results.quote: REINFORCE learns much more slowly than RL methods using value functions and has received relatively little attention.

limits: No experiments; purely theoretical, so no empirical evidence of speed or variance benefits.
Convergence is to a local optimum only, and Theorem 3 is for a form of policy iteration that assumes f_w is solved to its exact fixed point each iteration.
Requires compatibility condition (4), which restricts the critic's form; practical critics usually violate it.
Assumes a stationary state distribution independent of s0 and bounded rewards and second derivatives.
Authors present this as a first step toward proving convergence of actor-critic algorithms; actor-critic convergence itself is not proved.

terms.definition: f_w with df_w/dw = (dpi/dtheta)(1/pi), so that the critic's error is orthogonal to the policy gradient

lineage.note: REINFORCE shown to follow the gradient in expectation; paper adds learned value function
